scores.author: Werner
scores.why: Recessions are chosen: “whenever we see a country in recession, this is a policy-decision by the central planners”.

scores.author: Krainer
scores.why: A “monolithic and ruthless conspiracy” with a hidden hand.

scores.author: Berletic
scores.why: A plan, written down: “US policy papers explicitly lay out plans for maritime blockades, attacking the Chinese BRI”.

scores.author: Dixon
scores.why: “There is no one on top. It’s not an organized cabal.”

scores.author: Fitts
scores.why: Both: “Oh, there’s total malice”, yet “the people who run the financial system are first and foremost risk managers”, “very afraid of the guillotine”.

scores.author: Norton
scores.why: Class interest acting in the open: “US government policy is made by and for these powerful corporations.”

scores.author: Henningsen
scores.why: A regime-change “formula”, but of the Iran war: “if this is some grandmaster plan, can someone explain to me what is in America’s interest”.

scores.author: Martenson
scores.why: Undecided: “they know not what they do”, or “maybe they did it”.

scores.author: Hudson
scores.why: “There has been a long plan”, stated openly: “no attempt to conceal it”.

scores.author: Crooke
scores.why: Behind Trump, “a clear design for the preservation of a certain power structure’s ambition to attain global primacy”.

scores.author: Wilkerson
scores.why: Mostly incompetence, careerism and hatred: “There is no strategic purpose to it.”

scores.author: Diesen
scores.why: Structure more than plan: “A declining hegemon will predictably seek to weaken rising powers.”

scores.author: Webb
scores.why: “A handful of men with bottomless pockets who were willing to wait decades.”

scores.author: Wolff
scores.why: Class interest and a declining empire, not a hidden plan; government is an arena where “clumps” of capitalists “work out amongst themselves a deal”.

scores.author: Werner
scores.why: Central banks and bank credit: “the tools are available to quickly exit any recession and deliver high growth and prosperity for all.”

scores.author: Krainer
scores.why: “The bankers hold all the power.”

scores.author: Berletic
scores.why: “Wall Street and Washington”: arms, energy and tech using the state.

scores.author: Dixon
scores.why: Asset managers sit across the market, though Larry Fink is “not the top of the chain”; BlackRock “doesn’t have a monopoly”.

scores.author: Fitts
scores.why: The financial system’s managers “print money out of thin air” and are “increasingly above the law”.

scores.author: Norton
scores.why: Oligarchs and corporations; through Hudson on his site, “an extractive, predatory financial system”.

scores.author: Henningsen
scores.why: Old money, insurers and donors rather than banks alone: “Most of the money in this city is concentrated into old money and foreign money”.

scores.author: Martenson
scores.why: Banks make money “out of thin air” and the Fed moves wealth upward, but energy sits underneath.

scores.author: Hudson
scores.why: A rentier class has run governments through their finances since medieval times: “the birth of the fiscal state—a state that is governed above all by its fiscal policy that is dominated by the banking class itself”.

scores.author: Crooke
scores.why: Finance is the enforcer: a “dark state” bid for primacy, with the “financial oligarchy as its enforcement structure”.

scores.author: Wilkerson
scores.why: The national security state, arms makers and donors; finance appears mainly as a debt warning: “The bond market is saying Trump is going to have one of the worst economic situations by midterm in our history.”

scores.author: Diesen
scores.why: Says little about money; power is the hegemon’s project, “a world order defined as liberal hegemony”.

scores.author: Webb
scores.why: “A world system of financial control in private hands” (quoting Quigley), joined to intelligence and tech.

scores.author: Wolff
scores.why: The employer class as a whole; business lobbies speak for “a clump of American enterprises who have carved out a niche for themselves”.

scores.author: Werner
scores.why: Small local banks against the central planners: “Who lends to small firms? It’s small banks and that’s it.”

scores.author: Krainer
scores.why: A sovereign state over the oligarchs: “We, the people, must demand sovereignty and empower ourselves to plan a future rooted in a genuine love of humanity.”

scores.author: Berletic
scores.why: A multipolar world of sovereign states, against “Wall Street and Washington’s pursuit of a unipolar world order and its war on the emerging multipolar world”.

scores.author: Dixon
scores.why: Boycott and exit: “If you want to boycott BlackRock, you have to own it in self custody.”

scores.author: Fitts
scores.why: Personal and local: “You can use cash. Okay. And you can stop shopping. You can stop using the banks.”

scores.author: Norton
scores.why: Multipolarity and de-dollarised trade; on his site Radhika Desai argues for “some version of capital controls”.

scores.author: Henningsen
scores.why: National and energy sovereignty, yet against global taxation: “a form of global collectivism, or communism”.

scores.author: Martenson
scores.why: Personal and local: “for ordinary people, having some buffers in your life is can make sense”; gold, land, food and neighbours.

scores.author: Hudson
scores.why: Credit as “a public utility” under a central authority; tax land rent; write down unpayable debts.

scores.author: Crooke
scores.why: Civilisational sovereignty, “self-circulating, self-sufficient economies” and a defensive concert of powers.

scores.author: Wilkerson
scores.why: Diplomacy and restraint: “We are either going to go back to offshore balancing, which we should, never should have abandoned it”; and an amendment to undo Citizens United.

scores.author: Diesen
scores.why: Diplomacy: “understand their security concerns, and then find ways to mitigate security competition and pursue forms of indivisible security”.

scores.author: Webb
scores.why: Exposure, with no personal programme in what I read; “The decentralization theater… is masking the greatest centralization of power in history”.

scores.author: Wolff
scores.why: Neither exit nor the state: “Democratically organized worker cooperatives are the goal”, for private and state-owned enterprises alike.

scores.author: Werner
scores.why: Deng’s reforms are the model: China’s rise “to superpower status in only 40 years can teach us much”; Mao’s era is the warning.

scores.author: Krainer
scores.why: “The most undeniable case” for the national system.

scores.author: Berletic
scores.why: Pursuing abundance; align with it: “China has already committed to a national and global model of abundance.”

scores.author: Dixon
scores.why: A different model (“All the currency that’s printed goes back to the government and the government reinvests it in its own infrastructure”), but capital is “moving east” into it.

scores.author: Fitts
scores.why: Impressive (“very very impressive”), but “China was developed by Europe and US capital”, and she does not know “what obligations does China have to European and US capital”.

scores.author: Norton
scores.why: “The United States is capitalist and constitutes the heart of the capitalist world-system, whereas China is socialist.”

scores.author: Henningsen
scores.why: Benign; has not “really done any harm”.

scores.author: Martenson
scores.why: Admires its energy planning; says it “does not care that much about human life”.

scores.author: Hudson
scores.why: Keeps money creation public; its property finance has caught “the American-British disease”.

scores.author: Crooke
scores.why: Winning the contest: “Beijing has prepared and built a fortress around one of the most critical inputs to modern technology”; containment is “probably already too late”.

scores.author: Wilkerson
scores.why: “China is winning”, and from his talks with its officials, does not want an American-style empire.

scores.author: Diesen
scores.why: A rising power that “can resist economic coercion”.

scores.author: Wolff
scores.why: “A remarkable mastery of both economic nationalism and openness”; warns of a road “toward a new Chinese global empire”.

scores.author: Werner
scores.why: The EU is “serious about wartime mobilisation and the digital Gulag”.

scores.author: Krainer
scores.why: Fears fraudulent money, but “blockchain could be as important to the transformation of the money system as the Arabic numerals have been to math and sciences”.

scores.author: Dixon
scores.why: A control layer being built: “we can progress our digital ID, we can progress our central bank digital currency”; self-custody is the exit.

scores.author: Fitts
scores.why: “The control grid”, with stablecoins as its rails.

scores.author: Norton
scores.why: Not a theme; crypto is a scam: “US politicians are promoting crypto rug pull scams, exploiting their own supporters.”

scores.author: Henningsen
scores.why: In 2022, the CBDC roll-out was “completely in line with the Great Reset’s digital global fiat and cashless society, with its digital ID wallets”; silent on it in 2026.

scores.author: Martenson
scores.why: AI, cameras and digital ID as “our control grid”; expects fuel rationing by digital currency.

scores.author: Hudson
scores.why: US AI is “police state type of technology”, but digital money is not his threat; stablecoins are unsafe because the US seizes them.

scores.author: Crooke
scores.why: Not a theme; he sees “compute and the minerals” as a new US choke point.

scores.author: Webb
scores.why: Trump would use “programmable, surveillable stablecoins to expand and entrench dollar dominance”; digital ID through UN goal SDG 16.9.

scores.author: Werner
scores.why: Israel has its own “intentions and goals”, which drain US resources.

scores.author: Krainer
scores.why: “The invention of the Brits”: an instrument of the City.

scores.author: Berletic
scores.why: “On behalf of Israel” is a myth.

scores.author: Dixon
scores.why: A proxy: “if you want to do something that’s really, really illegal, like a genocide or ethnic cleansing, then use your Israeli proxy”.

scores.author: Fitts
scores.why: Ties Israel to the hidden system: Forrestal “was very opposed to the creation of the black budget and the creation of Israel”.

scores.author: Norton
scores.why: Quotes Biden approvingly as proof of the relationship: “Israel is the best investment we make”; Hudson, on his site, calls Israel “a client army”.

scores.author: Henningsen
scores.why: “It’s a war for Israel.” The lobby picked the cabinet.

scores.author: Martenson
scores.why: Reports Joe Kent’s view that the lobby drove the war; Trump “became far more Israel-focused”.

scores.author: Hudson
scores.why: “Israel is a satellite of the United States”, which “could stop Israel at any time”.

scores.author: Crooke
scores.why: “The U.S.-Israeli war primordially is being waged to create Israeli hegemony across West Asia”; on Russia, “the veto of pro-Israel mega-donors”.

scores.author: Wilkerson
scores.why: “Israel’s our tool, not the other way around”, yet Trump is “trapped by Netanyahu” and donor money.

scores.author: Diesen
scores.why: Israel would “pull America into one of its wars”; Trump may be “beholden to Netanyahu”.

scores.author: Webb
scores.why: A partnership: a “CIA-Israeli intelligence nexus”.

scores.author: Wolff
scores.why: The wars are US-led; AIPAC money keeps both parties in line; Israel attempts “17th century colonialism … several centuries too late”.

scores.author: Werner
scores.why: The dollar system: the war is “the attempt to ensure that the petro dollar can survive”.

scores.author: Krainer
scores.why: “All wars are bankers’ wars… It is strictly about banking and about the collateral.”

scores.author: Berletic
scores.why: The US state gains even when it seems to lose: “the US is conducting a “controlled demolition”” of Asia’s energy supply.

scores.author: Dixon
scores.why: “The military companies, their stock price benefits, the more wars you can go in.”

scores.author: Fitts
scores.why: Whoever owns the stock: policy that moves a dollar into a listed company multiplies it, “if I make a dollar, my stock goes up $10”.

scores.author: Norton
scores.why: Trump “is demonstrating to the world that all US wars are indeed a form of class war.”

scores.author: Henningsen
scores.why: The arms makers are “profiting massively”, while “accelerating the demise of the very empire” they serve.

scores.author: Martenson
scores.why: Asks whether the shortage itself is the aim: “I’m starting to wonder if that hasn’t been the point all along.”

scores.author: Hudson
scores.why: “Donald Trump’s war is to make money for himself, and he makes money by essentially manipulating the stock market prices.”

scores.author: Crooke
scores.why: Framed as a contest between states: “The U.S. has lost the war.”

scores.author: Wilkerson
scores.why: Of the arms makers: “They know they’re going to make money out their yin yang.” He still frames the war as a US defeat.

scores.author: Diesen
scores.why: Framed as a contest between states: “Iran has triumphantly defeated the US”.

scores.author: Wolff
scores.why: “Wars accelerate contracts to replace used-up arms and thereby profit military-industrial complexes.”

scores.author: Werner
scores.why: Welcomed the challenge to the Fed (August 2025): “President Trump has challenged the powerful Federal Reserve head-on.”

scores.author: Krainer
scores.why: “Real, not controlled, opposition” (October 2025).

scores.author: Berletic
scores.why: “Continuity of agenda”, whoever is president.

scores.author: Dixon
scores.why: Expected peace seven weeks before the war: “I think Iran has already been regime changed.”

scores.author: Fitts
scores.why: Tracks his administration as the builder of the control grid (April 2025): “A complete reengineering of the U.S. government through the digital systems is now possible at high speed.”

scores.author: Norton
scores.why: Trump “claims to be a so-called “peace president”, but he has bombed more countries than any other US leader.”

scores.author: Henningsen
scores.why: 2016: “the outsider eventually becomes the insider”.

scores.author: Martenson
scores.why: Trump “seemed to be on track”, and “then something shifted”.

scores.author: Hudson
scores.why: “A uniparty with two personalities”; he dates the plan to 2018. No pre-war text read.

scores.author: Crooke
scores.why: In 2025 a possible disruptor (“Trump as Myth”), then “wholly co-opted” on Russia.

scores.author: Wilkerson
scores.why: Nov 2024, on Trump’s “disdain for war. I think it’s genuine”, but Israel was the danger.

scores.author: Diesen
scores.why: Sceptical in March 2025; by July 2025 Trump is “very much aligned with the hawks”.

scores.author: Webb
scores.why: July 2024: “the Trump administration was responsible for implementing the BlackRock-designed “Going Direct Reset.”” and would push stablecoins next.

scores.author: Wolff
scores.why: Jan 2025: “whatever he in fact does is marginal”; his “capacity for saying one thing and doing another is already legendary”.

scores.author: Werner
scores.why: June 2026: “The true aim is to make war on China.” Later: an attempt to keep the petrodollar alive.

scores.author: Berletic
scores.why: Iran, Russia and Venezuela are steps toward China; cutting Asia’s energy gives “the US strategic leverage over Asia to create a similar united front against China”.

scores.author: Dixon
scores.why: Not a war on China; before it began he said “Iran has already been regime changed and the IRGC are completely on board”.

scores.author: Fitts
scores.why: “Iran right now is the big leakage in the system”; its oil “feeding China gives China greater independence”.

scores.author: Norton
scores.why: “The ultimate goal of isolating Beijing.”

scores.author: Henningsen
scores.why: “A war for Israel”; China will “sit back and watch”.

scores.author: Martenson
scores.why: China is “the country that we’re going to hit the most”, but he suspects the shortage itself may be the point.

scores.author: Hudson
scores.why: An oil war for choke-point control; China is “the number one enemy”.

scores.author: Crooke
scores.why: “All about a bigger U.S. play”: control chokepoints to deny China energy, alongside Israeli hegemony.

scores.author: Wilkerson
scores.why: Mainly for Israel and from hatred, but the railway matters: “We’re bombing the hell out of that railroad that China had finished all the way to the Persian Gulf”.

scores.author: Diesen
scores.why: US wars on Russia, Iran and China aim “to knock out or roll back the key adversaries on the Eurasian continent”.

scores.author: Wolff
scores.why: A bid to reverse decline and “do another Maduro” in Iran; reports elites saying the real enemy at Hormuz is “a Chinese”.

scores.author: Werner
scores.why: BRICS settlement systems are “not linked to the dollar”, “not swift”; Deng’s China is his model.

scores.author: Krainer
scores.why: “Multipolar integrations: the other system.”

scores.author: Berletic
scores.why: The multipolar world is the remedy; the US wages a “war on multipolarism”.

scores.author: Dixon
scores.why: “BlackRock wants to split the world up into a multipolar world order. That’s the next empire.” Sovereign states can still use their own resources.

scores.author: Fitts
scores.why: Not a clean alternative: “China was developed by Europe and US capital”, with obligations she cannot see.

scores.author: Norton
scores.why: “China wants a multipolar order based on peace, sovereign equality, and win-win cooperation.”

scores.author: Henningsen
scores.why: 2022: the blocs are diverging, “while Klaus and the West head towards their technocratic digital ‘utopia’”.

scores.author: Hudson
scores.why: “Forget the BRICS”, but China, Russia and Iran form a real core. Warns China has caught “the American-British disease” in property.

scores.author: Crooke
scores.why: Civilisational states against a Western bid for primacy: “this moral, civilisational way-of-being versus the radical Trumpian-U.S. materialist void”.

scores.author: Wilkerson
scores.why: “China is winning” and does not want an American-style empire.

scores.author: Diesen
scores.why: A real alternative to hegemony: “Diplomacy between sovereign equals is replaced with the ‘civilizational teachers’ rewarding or punishing the ‘civilizational students’.”

scores.author: Webb
scores.why: One system: Pisar’s “transideological corporation”, with Western firms “merging and/ or forging significant agreements or joint ventures” with Eastern state firms.

scores.author: Wolff
scores.why: A real alternative: the BRICS’ “aggregate GDP surpassed that of the G7” in 2020, though the road could lead “toward a new Chinese global empire”.

scores.author: Werner
scores.why: “Power-hungry central planners who want to control us vs. the People”, at the central banks and around them.

scores.author: Krainer
scores.why: “The City of London with its satellites on Wall Street, in Paris, Frankfurt, Basel, Tokyo.”

scores.author: Berletic
scores.why: “Wall Street and Washington”: US interests using the US state.

scores.author: Dixon
scores.why: Asset managers and sovereign wealth funds: “we are in the asset stripping phase and the money’s moving east.”

scores.author: Fitts
scores.why: Investment networks around the central banks: “They’re sort of above countries.”

scores.author: Norton
scores.why: US oligarchs and corporations, through the US state: policy “is made by and for these powerful corporations”.

scores.author: Henningsen
scores.why: The City of London as much as Washington: “Most of the money in this city is concentrated into old money and foreign money… You could call that the colonial dividend.”

scores.author: Martenson
scores.why: A class “above” the president: “power brokers in DC” and Wall Street.

scores.author: Hudson
scores.why: That class now works through Washington’s leverage: “the American strategy can only succeed as long as the United States can impose choke points on the entire world”.

scores.author: Crooke
scores.why: A US “Dark State” whose ambitions are “one world governance”, with finance as its enforcer.

scores.author: Wilkerson
scores.why: The US “national security state”, arms makers and donors.

scores.author: Diesen
scores.why: The hegemon: “The West subsequently pursued a world order defined as liberal hegemony, in which the West would dominate the world rather than manage great-power balancing”.

scores.author: Webb
scores.why: “A world system of financial control in private hands”, run through public-private partnerships.

scores.author: Wolff
scores.why: The US employer class acting through the US state: “Both parties use the money from their major donors”.

scores.author: Krainer
scores.why: “We can vote for politicians, but the bankers hold all the power and we’ve no way to overturn their policies at the ballot box.”

scores.author: Berletic
scores.why: Party contests are “political theater used to perpetuate this continuity of agenda”.

scores.author: Dixon
scores.why: “You cannot fix this system through the ballot box because the politicians are owned by the lobbies.”

scores.author: Fitts
scores.why: Built a tool to let voters see federal money by district and “hold your congressman accountable”; her remedy now is local.

scores.author: Henningsen
scores.why: Big parties absorb protest movements into “the current two-party paradigm”; “the outsider eventually becomes the insider”.

scores.author: Martenson
scores.why: Agrees (“Exactly”) with Ratigan’s call for a political organisation “outside the two political parties”.

scores.author: Hudson
scores.why: “It doesn’t matter what the voters want because their choice is between two parties that have exactly the same position.”

scores.author: Crooke
scores.why: Policy “transcends party lines and is implemented regardless of which administration occupies the White House”.

scores.author: Wilkerson
scores.why: Law can still work: “We already have 26 states. We only need three-quarters of the states, two-thirds of the Congress.”

scores.author: Diesen
scores.why: “One can change the people in power, there’s often less and less ability to actually change the policies.”

scores.author: Wolff
scores.why: Elections matter when movements drive them: Mamdani’s win is “an index of change”; the Democratic centre blocks it.

scores.author: Werner
scores.why: An institutional class: “power-hungry central planners who want to control us vs. the People”.

scores.author: Krainer
scores.why: Finance, not countries: “all wars are bankers’ wars”.

scores.author: Berletic
scores.why: Both: “Wall Street and Washington’s pursuit of a unipolar world order”.

scores.author: Dixon
scores.why: “America is not a country; it is a series of companies and a financial industrial complex.”

scores.author: Fitts
scores.why: Networks: “They’re sort of above countries.”

scores.author: Norton
scores.why: A class acting through the state: “US government policy is made by and for these powerful corporations.”

scores.author: Henningsen
scores.why: Both: “The US empire is the dog”, with old money, insurers and the lobby inside it.

scores.author: Martenson
scores.why: “There’s a class of people above him, who have more power than the government because they are completely untouchable.”

scores.author: Hudson
scores.why: A creditor class running states: “a state that is governed above all by its fiscal policy that is dominated by the banking class itself”.

scores.author: Crooke
scores.why: Mostly civilisational states: “this moral, civilisational way-of-being versus the radical Trumpian-U.S. materialist void”, though with donors behind Trump.

scores.author: Wilkerson
scores.why: Mostly states and their officials: “Mark my words, we’re leaving. We are either going to go back to offshore balancing”.

scores.author: Diesen
scores.why: States: “A declining hegemon will predictably seek to weaken rising powers.”

scores.author: Webb
scores.why: “A world system of financial control in private hands”, quoting Quigley.

scores.author: Wolff
scores.why: Blocs: government “becomes the arena very vulgar of clumps subgroups of capitalists”.

scores.author: Mearsheimer
scores.why: Elites believe their own stories rather than plan a deception: “I don't think that's what's going on. I think it's much more unconscious.”

scores.author: Mearsheimer
scores.why: Power belongs to states: “spheres of influence are geographical regions that great powers dominate”.

scores.author: Mearsheimer
scores.why: Restraint and prioritising by a strong state: “understand how this world works. Understand the tragic nature of international politics and do everything you can to manage it.”

scores.author: Mearsheimer
scores.why: A formidable rival rather than a model: “this country is so impressive in terms of its economic might and now its military might as well.”

scores.author: Mearsheimer
scores.why: With Walt: “the thrust of US policy in the region derives almost entirely from domestic politics”, above all the Israel lobby.

scores.author: Mearsheimer
scores.why: Framed as a contest between states: “it's just very important to understand that Iran has won this war”.

scores.author: Mearsheimer
scores.why: The Iran war is not about China, though the Gulf is where the rivalry will play out: “the real competition will come in the Middle East”.

scores.author: Mearsheimer
scores.why: The US state, over-stretched: “the United States still labors under the illusion that it can be everywhere and do everything all the time.”

scores.author: Mearsheimer
scores.why: On Israel the debate is closed, with Walt: “Where Israel is concerned, however, potential critics fall silent.”

scores.author: Mearsheimer
scores.why: States and their power: “Iran is going to emerge from this war much more powerful relative to its neighbors”.

scores.author: Sachs
scores.why: A long plan by a network, executed on a whim: “the culmination of a long-standing plan by Israel and the US to dominate the Arab world and West Asia”.

scores.author: Sachs
scores.why: Power lies with states and leaders bent on hegemony: “the US and Israel are dead set on hegemony in the Arab world and West Asia”.

scores.author: Sachs
scores.why: States under international law: “The end result would be a return to international law and the UN Charter.”

scores.author: Sachs
scores.why: A rise to welcome: “the rise of China is a good thing and it will help the us”.

scores.author: Sachs
scores.why: Israel plans, the US carries it out: the Clean Break strategy “calls for Israel to establish hegemony in the region through wars of regime change, with the US as the implementing partner”.

scores.author: Sachs
scores.why: Framed as a contest between states: “The American empire cannot win the war against Iran at an acceptable financial, military, and political cost.”

scores.author: Sachs
scores.why: The war is Israel's project, but the sanctions target China: “Above all, the campaign is targeted against China, which buys more than 80 percent of Iran's oil exports.”

scores.author: Sachs
scores.why: A real alternative: “The BRICS have the credibility, the economic weight, and the absence of the historical complicity in Middle East imperialism to bring the world to its senses.”

scores.author: Sachs
scores.why: The US state chasing lost primacy: “The United States was attempting to preserve a global dominance that it no longer possesses”.

scores.author: Sachs
scores.why: Law still works: “the Supreme Court confirmed what many of us argued from the beginning: Your sweeping tariffs were an unlawful overreach of executive power.”

scores.author: Sachs
scores.why: Leaders and their psychology: “They are in the grip of three cascading pathologies. The first is personality”.

advice.advice: Read critically: ask who pays the speaker, and read the documents themselves
advice.author: Henningsen
advice.quote: Of Mike Pompeo: “he’s paid to have his views… who’s paying his grocery bill.”

advice.advice: Read critically: ask who pays the speaker, and read the documents themselves
advice.author: Berletic
advice.quote: Until “journalists, analysts, and the general public can strip away the political theater”, the agenda continues.

advice.advice: Hold assets outside the banks: gold, silver, commodities, Bitcoin or crypto
advice.author: Dixon
advice.quote: “If you want to boycott the Federal Reserve, then you have to own money outside the system. Gold or Bitcoin are two ways of doing that.”

advice.advice: Hold assets outside the banks: gold, silver, commodities, Bitcoin or crypto
advice.author: Martenson
advice.quote: “Individual resilience. Um buy gold, have some chickens, you know, stuff like that.”

advice.advice: Hold assets outside the banks: gold, silver, commodities, Bitcoin or crypto
advice.author: Krainer
advice.quote: 2023: “acquire some farmland (if possible), some gold and silver bullion” and commodity futures; crypto “holds potential to advance our emancipation from the current money prison”. By 2026 he calls gold, crypto and the like “merely temporary refuges”.

advice.advice: Organise or act politically
advice.author: Wilkerson
advice.quote: Backs a constitutional amendment to undo Citizens United: “We already have 26 states.”

advice.advice: Organise or act politically
advice.author: Krainer
advice.quote: “We can’t vote our way out of this matrix… This will have to be fought, sooner or later.”

advice.advice: Organise or act politically
advice.author: Martenson
advice.quote: Agrees (“Exactly”) with Dylan Ratigan that change needs a political organisation “outside the two political parties”.

advice.advice: Organise or act politically
advice.author: Wolff
advice.quote: To an organising meeting, January 2025: “Build on what you got … Work with us, with everybody else.” His longer-run aim: worker cooperatives.

advice.advice: Boycott: stop buying from, and banking with, the centralisers

cases.title: Blocs collide: big oil against big agriculture over diesel

happened.text: Diesel prices were squeezing farmers, so farm-state senators and large agricultural firms asked Trump to ban diesel exports.
happened.author: Wolff
Wolff
happened.quote: We have been your loyal supporters. We don't want this.

happened.author: Wolff

happened.text: The refiners threatened to cut output; the ban was dropped. The farmers got a release of European reserves worth about a day's demand.
happened.author: Wolff
happened.quote: we will cut back on refining and it'll go right back up

bears_on.reading: At this level policy was bargained between competing blocs, with the president as broker, not handed down by one plan. It fits more easily with the scores near the bottom of the scale (Wolff, Dixon, Wilkerson, Diesen) and with the nexus model in synthesis.md, and is harder to square with “one deliberate plan” (Krainer, Webb). It does not rule out a plan above this level.

forecasts: Hudson: Trump holds fuel prices down until the November vote
Martenson: oil pushed down before the midterms
cases.forecast_note: A refiners' veto on cheaper diesel cuts against both; neither is marked failed until the vote on 3 November.
cases.limits: One case, told by one author whose own verdict is “That seems to have worked”. It does not test the harder collision the nexus model names: the Israel lobby against finance or energy. The reading of what it fits is mine.

hypotheses.title: A nexus of interests
hypotheses.answers: Question 4: is anyone hidden at the top?
hypotheses.proposed_by: Dixon, Henningsen, Hudson and Wolff, each in part; combined into one model by the person who assembled these sources
hypotheses.claim: The US state is shared by interest blocs (finance, arms, energy, technology, the Israel lobby, media and think tanks). A policy happens when enough blocs want it and none strong enough objects; finance owns and funds the others.
hypotheses.evidence: Dixon's shared ownership, Henningsen's blocs, Hudson's choke points, Wolff's "clumps" of capitalists bargaining over the state.
hypotheses.objection: Krainer and Webb see one directing group; Norton sees one class; Crooke sees a project behind the blocs.
tests: Policy stalls or reverses where blocs collide
The Israel lobby against finance or energy
hypotheses.status: One case fits: the diesel collision (October 2026), where the oil bloc beat agriculture. The harder test has not occurred.

hypotheses.title: Energy dominance by managed demolition
hypotheses.answers: Question 8: whose war is the Iran war?
hypotheses.proposed_by: Berletic, most of it; Hudson, Wilkerson and Werner add pieces; combined by the person who assembled these sources
hypotheses.claim: The Iran war aims to close the Gulf with deniability, making Europe and Asia dependent on US energy, as Ukraine and Nord Stream did for Europe; Israel's Mediterranean routes and gas fit the same aim.
hypotheses.evidence: Berletic's "decades-spanning US project"; Hudson's choke points and Arctic logic; Wilkerson's base withdrawal; the canal proposal, Gaza Marine and the 2023 gas licences. The deniability is on paper: the 2009 Brookings chapter "Leave it to Bibi". Werner: "the US military leadership essentially ordered many US bases in the region to be evacuated."
hypotheses.objection: It can explain any outcome. Its costs fall on the population and on the dollar's Treasury market, as the Gulf states buy less US debt; but if finance is global and moving east, as Dixon argues, it may lose nothing while the country is stripped.
tests: US share of Europe's and Asia's gas imports
Mediterranean pipeline, canal or Gaza Marine
Gulf supply impaired while American supply fills the gap
Gulf bases cut, Arctic deployments grown
No durable deal reopens Hormuz

hypotheses.title: A hidden directing hand
hypotheses.claim: A small group, centred on finance, directs events over decades, mostly out of view.
hypotheses.evidence: Webb's documented networks of the same financiers and intelligence figures; Krainer's history of the City of London.
hypotheses.objection: The insiders here (Fitts, Hudson, Dixon, Wilkerson, Tyson) each describe one part from inside; none describes a central body. Webb's links show proximity better than intent.
tests: A document or insider describing a directing body, not only overlapping networks
hypotheses.status: Not supported by the insider testimony in this set; not ruled out.

hypotheses.title: A ruling class acting in the open
hypotheses.claim: An employer and creditor class rules through donors and the state, mostly openly; plans are written down.
hypotheses.evidence: Norton: US policy is "made by and for these powerful corporations". Wolff: the same donors fund both parties. Hudson: officials state their aims openly.
hypotheses.objection: It says little about the secret side: Fitts's covert economy and the off-books budget.
tests: Whether stated plans and donor interests predict policy better than hidden ones
hypotheses.status: Consistent with the diesel case and with the forecast record below.

hypotheses.title: The logic of a declining hegemon
hypotheses.claim: No hidden ruler is needed: a hegemon losing its rival behaves predictably, over-extending and turning on its allies.
hypotheses.evidence: Diesen's forecast that a war on Iran would be a disaster held; Wolff's account of tariffs and tribute as desperate acts.
hypotheses.objection: It treats states as the actors and wars as won or lost by countries. On the bloc reading no country acts: policies that look "irrational" for a state are rational for whoever profits, and the arms and finance complexes gain whether a war is won or lost. It also says little about money.
tests: Whether US behaviour keeps matching what decline predicts, for example turning on more allies
hypotheses.status: Its forecasts on the war held.

hypotheses.title: A written plan, followed through
hypotheses.claim: US policy follows plans laid out in policy papers, whichever party is in power; apparent defeats advance the plan.
hypotheses.evidence: The best forecast record on Trump and the Iran war; the plans are on paper.
hypotheses.objection: Henningsen cannot see what US interest the Iran war serves; Wilkerson thinks a plan can live in the planners without the president.
tests: Whether the next moves match the published papers
hypotheses.status: Best forecast record in the set so far.

hypotheses.title: A war for Israel
hypotheses.claim: The Iran war serves Israel, not the US; the Israel lobby steers US policy in West Asia.
hypotheses.evidence: No US interest that Henningsen can find; Crooke's "primordially" for Israeli hegemony; pro-Israel donors.
hypotheses.objection: Chomsky's 2006 test: where the lobby and US interests diverged, Israel backed down. And the appearance may be designed: the 2009 Brookings paper's chapter "Leave it to Bibi" proposed letting Israel strike so that criticism and retaliation would be "deflected away from the United States and onto Israel". It warned that this would be hard to sell, since Iranians would see the strike as "American supported or even American orchestrated", flown in US-funded aircraft.
tests: A case where Israel's aims and the energy or finance bloc's aims diverge
hypotheses.status: Contested. If the Brookings logic is being followed, a war that looks like Israel's is what the planners intended, so the appearance cannot count as evidence for H7; and it cannot be separated from H2 while the interests run together.

hypotheses.title: Mobile finance, anchored arms
hypotheses.proposed_by: Dixon (finance moving east), with Crooke and Wilkerson on the arms complex; combined by the person who assembled these sources
hypotheses.claim: The blocs differ in how easily they move. The arms complex is tied to US territory, entrenched in costly, outdated weapons, and has been shown up by cheap drones and missiles. Finance needs no physical location and is moving east. As military power stops being concentrated in the US, the US matters less to the bloc that owns the others.
hypotheses.evidence: Crooke: "small, fleeter Iranian naval assets ran rings around the large lumbering naval vessels of the U.S. Navy". Wilkerson: "our maritime assets are getting increasingly dated". Dixon: "the money's moving east". Wolff: the US as "a place where you can safely keep your money is finished". Fitts: "They're sort of above countries."
hypotheses.objection: Finance needs a guard for its contracts and choke points. Crooke: "dollar hegemony largely is a function of preserving the myth of U.S. exceptional military invulnerability"; Hudson: the strategy works only "as long as the United States can impose choke points". If the arms complex fails, finance must find a new protector, and where it goes is the test.
tests: Official holders outside the West cut Treasuries and buy gold (met)
Total foreign holdings of US Treasuries fall (not so far: a record in June 2026)
Asian financial centres gain listings and assets
Large asset managers shift headquarters, staff or new funds to Asia
US procurement keeps favouring carriers and jets over cheap drones and missiles
Finance aligns with a new military guarantor rather than the US
hypotheses.status: Mixed. Official holders outside the West are leaving Treasuries for gold (public data, 2026), but total foreign holdings hit a record in June 2026 as private buyers and the UK bought more. Other tests open.

hypotheses.title: Land against sea: the new Great Game
hypotheses.answers: Questions 6 and 8: the multipolar bloc, and whose war
hypotheses.proposed_by: Werner, Wilkerson, Diesen and Berletic; restated by the person who assembled these sources
hypotheses.claim: The European and US empires were sea-based, so controlling sea lanes was everything. A Eurasia joined by land corridors (railways, pipelines, the Belt and Road) as well as sea lanes would escape that control. Stopping such corridors has been a constant aim, from the world wars, fought partly to stop Germany building eastward toward Middle East oil, to the bombing of China's new railway through Iran in 2026.
hypotheses.evidence: Werner on 1914: "Germany's economic success & transport corridor plans were seen as lethal challenge to British hegemony requiring total war", and 2026 as "a replay" (the full argument is behind his paywall). Wilkerson: "We're bombing the hell out of that railroad that China had finished all the way to the Persian Gulf", because "most of the world's commerce travels over land". Diesen on Mackinder's fear of Russia's "intercontinental railways". Henningsen: "US maritime power is in many ways backstopped by the city of London", whose insurers reach sea trade but not land routes. Berletic: US papers plan "maritime blockades, attacking the Chinese BRI".
hypotheses.objection: Dixon and Webb would say the corridors change the route, not the owner: the same capital buys into the land routes. The reply is physical. Sea trade runs through a few choke points that a navy can hold; a dense rail network across a continent, like China's today, cannot be stopped without bombing the whole continent. Owning capital does not settle who controls the routes, much as Martenson argues that energy, not money, sets the limits.
tests: Freight on China-Europe and China-Iran rail corridors grows despite strikes
Further strikes or sanctions aimed at rail and pipeline corridors rather than military targets
Western funds or insurers take large stakes in the land corridors (would support the objection)
Traffic on the Arctic route grows, with Russian and Chinese control
hypotheses.status: Proposed October 2026; Werner and Wilkerson tie the 1914 and 2026 cases to corridors; tests open.

hypotheses.title: The plan meets reality
hypotheses.answers: Questions 5 and 6: who gains from the wars, and whether the empire can hold
hypotheses.proposed_by: Crooke, Wilkerson, Hudson and Wolff; restated by the person who assembled these sources
hypotheses.claim: The Iran war can be part of a deliberate plan for US energy dominance and still fail when the plan meets reality. Nobody expected Iran's weapons to be what they proved to be: a new generation of drones and ballistic and guided missiles, made at home, kept underground, and aimed with Chinese and Russian satellite data. New technology can shift the balance of power, as Jared Diamond's Guns, Germs, and Steel shows over the long run of history. The US has de-industrialised and cannot match its rivals' arms production, so it needs short, decisive wars against weak opponents, and this is not one. Its arms industry was built to make profits, not to beat twenty-first-century adversaries. The old empire is in denial and doubling down while the world economy spirals.
hypotheses.evidence: Public data on munitions: CSIS estimates that Patriot stocks fell by at least 65% and THAAD by at least 38%, and that rebuilding them will take at least three years; THAAD interceptors were shipped from South Korea after Iran destroyed at least ten US radars, four of them THAAD radars; Gulf states ran low on interceptors; with the Bahrain base hit, carriers were resupplied from Diego Garcia; Patriots meant for Ukraine were diverted. From the authors: Crooke, four days in: "Iran sits in the driving seat", its fastest missiles "largely impervious to Israeli air defences". Wilkerson on the arms makers: they "know they're going to make money out their yin yang"; and on the response: "We don't back away. We don't retrench." Hudson: "Invasions don't work. All you can do is destroy other countries." Wolff on denial: "a refusal to entertain the very idea the empire is over".
hypotheses.objection: Failing for whom? Those the war pays profit whether it is won or lost (the 'profit either way' reading), and the energy-sales part is working: the US share of Europe's LNG keeps rising. The reply: an arms industry built for profit is exactly why the plan cannot win a long war against a capable adversary. The plan can enrich its contractors and still fail as a plan for dominance.
tests: Iran keeps launching at scale late in the war, showing its stocks and underground production survived
US output of interceptors and strike missiles (THAAD, SM-6, Tomahawk) stays below wartime use through 2027
After setbacks, Washington escalates (blockades, new sanctions, new fronts) rather than settles
The US share of the EU's LNG imports keeps rising (this would support 'on track' for the energy part)
hypotheses.status: Proposed October 2026; in the evidence grid 'on track' has the most facts against it, while 'failing' and 'profit either way' have few and can both be true; tests open.

hypotheses.label: No coherent aim: a blunder by a declining power

ach.note: The fact list was fixed before scoring and includes facts each side's authors put forward. Authors' interpretations are not facts here; only documents, public data, and what authors report as having happened. Facts marked as possibly staged are ones a capable actor could arrange for appearances. This grid asks only what the war is for. Whether the plan is working is a separate question, weighed in the next grid.

ach.question: Is the plan working?

hypotheses.label: On track: the plan is advancing as designed
Failing on contact: new weapons, a hollowed-out industrial base, a war that will not stay short
Profit either way: the outcome does not matter to those the war pays
hypotheses.from: Hudson, Wolff; the 'Who gains from the wars?' axis

ach.note: An explanation of what a war is for can be right while the plan fails. This grid assumes a purposeful plan (the first grid's best fits) and asks whether it is working. The munitions and logistics facts are public data, widely reported; the rest are authors' reports.

facts.text: Iran's fastest missiles got through Israeli air defences.
facts.author: Crooke
facts.quote: Iranian high-end missiles flying at speeds above Mach Four are proving largely impervious to Israeli air defences

reasons.O1: Defences that do not stop the main threat are not part of a plan going well.

facts.text: Killing the Supreme Leader rallied support for the Iranian state instead of toppling it.
facts.author: Crooke
facts.quote: it led instead to massive outpourings of support for the Islamic Republic

reasons.O1: The decapitation was meant to bring the state down.

facts.text: US interceptor stocks fell steeply: Patriot from about 2,330 before the war to 760–830, THAAD from 452 to 234–278 even after some resupply.
facts.source: CSIS estimates, reported by ABC News and Arab News (2026)

reasons.O1: A plan cannot run on munitions it is using up faster than it makes them.

facts.text: Replacing the Patriot, THAAD and Tomahawk stocks will take at least three years; Patriot output is about 600 a year.

reasons.O1: Only a short war fits stocks that take years to rebuild, and this one was not short.

facts.text: The arms makers expect large profits from the replacement orders.
facts.author: Wilkerson
facts.quote: They know they're going to make money out their yin yang

facts.text: The Pentagon's cost estimate is mostly for repairing or replacing equipment.
facts.author: Werner
facts.quote: most of this seems to consist of “repair or replacement costs for equipment”

facts.text: Iran's targeting appears to use Chinese satellite intelligence, with Russian backup.
facts.author: Wilkerson
facts.quote: With the help of a very sophisticated Chinese satellite, and probably backups from Russia

reasons.O1: A plan that isolates Iran would not leave it with real-time intelligence from China and Russia.

facts.text: The US share of the EU's LNG imports keeps rising (59% in 2026).

reasons.O2: The energy-sales part of the plan is succeeding in Europe.

facts.text: EU imports of Russian LNG hit a quarterly record in early 2026.

reasons.O1: Energy dominance means Europe buying less Russian gas, not more.

facts.text: During the ceasefire, the US imposed a naval blockade on Iranian shipping instead of settling.
facts.author: Werner
facts.quote: a US-led naval blockade

facts.text: The war's diesel prices split Trump's own backers, big oil against big agriculture, and nobody got relief.
facts.author: Wolff
facts.quote: One group of his supporters want it, another group of his supporters don't want it.

facts.text: Central banks outside the West are cutting US Treasuries and buying gold.

reasons.O1: A plan restoring US dominance would strengthen confidence in US assets; official holders outside the West are leaving them.

facts.text: THAAD interceptors were shipped from South Korea to the Middle East to make up the losses.
facts.source: US Forces Korea commander; Korea Times (March 2026)

reasons.O1: Stripping another theatre's defences shows the plan did not budget for this war.

facts.text: US interceptors carried most of Israel's defence (about 200 THAAD and over 100 SM-3 and SM-6, against Israel's own 100 Arrow and 90 David's Sling), while the Gulf states ran low (the UAE used up to three-quarters of its Patriots) and asked Washington to speed deliveries.
facts.source: Libertarian Institute, summarising US reporting; IDSA; CBS News (2026)

reasons.O1: The shield was stretched so thin that it covered Israel first and left the Gulf oil states short.

facts.text: With the US Navy base in Bahrain largely destroyed, the carriers had to be resupplied from Diego Garcia, Singapore or through Suez.

reasons.O1: Supply lines thousands of miles long were not the plan for a Gulf war.

facts.text: Patriot interceptors meant for Ukraine were diverted; in June Ukraine stopped only 14 of 54 Russian ballistic missiles.

reasons.O1: One theatre can only be fed by starving another: the industrial base cannot supply both.

facts.text: Hormuz is averaging almost 13 million barrels a day against about 20 million before the war, on the US Energy Secretary's own figures, while the president claims record flows.
facts.author: Johnson
facts.quote: The running average today is almost 13 million barrels a day

reasons.O1: The strait the plan depends on is running at about two-thirds of normal, and the administration has to dress that up as a record.

facts.text: Middle East net diesel exports were 390,000 barrels a day in August, just over a quarter of prewar levels (IEA figures, via Karl Miller).
facts.author: Johnson
facts.quote: just over a quarter of prewar levels

facts.text: Qatar puts repairs to two damaged LNG trains at about three years; Miller estimates up to five years for the worst-damaged Gulf facilities.
facts.author: Johnson
facts.quote: puts repairs to two damaged LNG trains at about three years

facts.text: US distillate exports hit a record 1.935 million barrels a day in early August, with refineries at 96.8% of capacity and East Coast stocks at record lows (EIA figures, via Karl Miller).
facts.author: Johnson
facts.quote: after a record 1.935 million in early August

facts.text: Since March the US has supplied more than half of Europe's diesel imports, two-thirds in August and September; in October Washington threatened an export ban until the G7 agreed to release 100 million barrels of reserves (Johnson, drawing on Karl Miller).
facts.author: Johnson
facts.quote: It is taking orders
